tactics.title: Sentinum: Fabius waits, Decius devotes himself

units.label: Decius: legions V and VI with allies
Fabius: legions I and III with allies
Reserve: L. Scipio and C. Marcius

phases.text: After two days of waiting, the armies formed up on the plain below Sentinum. Livy (10.27) puts the Gauls on the coalition right and the Samnites on the left, so Decius with legions V and VI faced the Gauls and Fabius with I and III faced the Samnites. The Etruscans and Umbrians were absent: Fabius had ordered Fulvius and Postumius to raid the territory of Clusium, and those contingents marched home. Livy thought their presence would have meant a Roman defeat. The consuls had agreed opposite plans: Fabius would fight defensively and let the Samnite and Gallic first rush burn out, Decius would attack.

Decius threw his cavalry at the Gallic horse and drove it back twice. On the second charge the Roman squadrons ran on into the enemy infantry and were struck by something new to them: war chariots and carts (essedis carrisque, Livy 10.28) driven in with a roar of wheels and hooves. The horses bolted, the cavalry came back through its own legions, and the Gallic infantry followed up into the disorder. With his wing breaking, Decius called the pontifex M. Livius, recited the formula of devotio dedicating himself and the enemy army to the Earth and the gods of the dead, and rode into the Gallic ranks to his death, as his father had at Veseris in 340.

phases.t: Fabius feeds the left and turns the Samnites
phases.text: Livy says the left recovered once Decius was dead: Livius took command and the troops collected the javelins littering the ground and showered the Gauls, who had locked their shields into a testudo. Fabius, told of the crisis, sent his reserve under L. Cornelius Scipio and C. Marcius across to the left. On his own wing the Samnites were now tiring, so he ordered the cavalry round the Samnite flank and the infantry forward. Losses show where the battle had been decided: Livy gives 7,000 dead in Decius' army and 1,700 in Fabius'.

phases.t: Samnite flight, the testudo broken, the camp stormed
phases.text: The Samnites broke and streamed back past the flank of the Gauls towards their camp. Fabius sent the 500 Campanian horse round the Gallic rear with the principes of legion III behind them, and the testudo, hit front and back, came apart. Fabius himself pressed on to the Samnite camp, where Gellius Egnatius was killed fighting at the gate. Livy's totals are 25,000 enemy dead and 8,000 captured against 8,700 Romans. He also notes, and rejects, writers who inflated the enemy to 60,000 foot, 40,000 horse and 1,000 chariots.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Livy 10.27-30, the only narrative. The site in the basin below Sassoferrato is conventional, not proven. Unit frontages, the reserve's position and the routes of the flanking cavalry are schematic; Livy's casualty figures probably derive from annalists and are not reliable in detail.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967)

tactics.title: Heraclea: the legions meet the phalanx and the elephants

phases.text: Pyrrhus had camped on the plain between Pandosia and Heraclea, hoping to delay until his Italian allies arrived, and posted light troops along the Siris. The consul P. Valerius Laevinus would not wait. Plutarch (Pyrrhus 16) says the infantry crossed at the fords while the cavalry splashed over at many points along the river, so that Pyrrhus' outposts, fearing encirclement, fell back. This is the first time a Roman army met a professional Hellenistic army, and Pyrrhus, watching the orderly crossing, is supposed to have remarked that the barbarians' discipline was not barbarous.

Pyrrhus led his horse guard into the Roman cavalry as it came up the bank, hoping to catch it before the infantry formed, and ordered the phalanx to deploy. The cavalry action was confused and personal: an Italian (Plutarch names Oplacus, a Frentanian) marked the king out and killed his horse, and Pyrrhus exchanged cloak and armour with Megacles, one of his Companions. The Roman cavalry held long enough for the legions to cross and deploy.

Phalanx and legions now fought on the plain north of the river. Plutarch says the struggle swayed seven times. Megacles, wearing the king's cloak, was cut down and his armour paraded, and the rumour that Pyrrhus was dead shook the phalanx until the king rode bareheaded along the line. For the Romans the phalanx's hedge of pikes was new; for Pyrrhus the legion, which fought in small units and could replace tired men from the rear lines, was new. Neither side broke.

Pyrrhus then brought his 20 elephants round against the Roman cavalry, whose horses would not face beasts they had never seen. The cavalry broke and fled into its own infantry, and Pyrrhus launched the Thessalian horse into the disorder. The Roman army collapsed back over the Siris. Hieronymus of Cardia, Pyrrhus' contemporary, put Roman losses at about 7,000 dead and 1,800 captured and Pyrrhus' at about 4,000; Dionysius gives 15,000 and 13,000. Pyrrhus had lost many of his best officers and men, which could not be replaced from Epirus.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Plutarch, who drew on Hieronymus of Cardia and Pyrrhus' memoirs. The exact place on the Siris near Policoro is uncertain, and no source gives Pyrrhus' order of battle; the wing positions of the elephants and Thessalians are inferred from the course of events.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Champion, Pyrrhus of Epirus (2009)

tactics.title: Ausculum: wagons against elephants

units.label: Left: Aetolian and Acarnanian mercenaries, Samnites

phases.t: The second day, on level ground
phases.text: On the first day the armies fought on broken, wooded ground near a river where neither the phalanx nor the elephants could work, and night ended an even fight. Overnight Pyrrhus occupied the rough ground with light troops, so on the second day the battle was fought on the open plain. Dionysius (20.1) gives his line from right to left: Macedonians, Italian mercenaries, Ambraciots, Tarentines with white shields, Bruttians and Lucanians, Thesprotians and Chaonians in the centre, then Aetolian, Acarnanian and Athamanian mercenaries, and Samnites on the left, with cavalry on both wings and elephants and light troops behind them. The Romans had built 300 wagons carrying poles with tridents, scythes and fire-pots to fight the elephants.

The wagons went forward against the place where the elephants had stood, but Pyrrhus had moved them, and his light troops and archers shot down the wagon crews and their oxen. Along the main front the fighting was hard and long. Dionysius says the Roman first legion pushed back the Macedonians and that the Pyrrhic centre, where the Italians stood, gave ground.

phases.t: The Daunian raid on Pyrrhus' camp
phases.text: At this point 4,000 foot and 400 horse of Rome's Daunian allies from Arpi, who had lost their way to the battlefield, came on Pyrrhus' camp from behind and plundered and burned it. Pyrrhus detached some elephants and cavalry against them; the Daunians took refuge on a steep height, and the detachment was then turned against the Roman line.

With the elephants committed against the Roman wing, the line broke and fell back to the camp across the stream. Night ended the fighting. Hieronymus, as preserved by Plutarch (Pyrrhus 21), gave 6,000 Roman and 3,505 Pyrrhic dead, the latter figure taken from the king's own records. Pyrrhus was wounded by a javelin in the arm. His reply to congratulations, that one more such victory would undo him, made this the original Pyrrhic victory. Later Roman tradition (Cicero, Zonaras) claimed that the consul P. Decius Mus devoted himself here as his father and grandfather had done, but this is doubtful.

tactics.note: Order of battle follows Dionysius 20.1, the fullest account, which is fragmentary; Plutarch's version (from Hieronymus) is shorter and differs in emphasis. The location near Ascoli Satriano and the river are approximate, and where exactly the elephants broke the Roman line is not stated. Day 1 is summarised in the first phase rather than drawn.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Champion, Pyrrhus of Epirus (2009)

tactics.title: Beneventum: the failed night march

phases.text: Back from Sicily with a depleted army, Pyrrhus split his forces, sending part to hold the consul L. Cornelius Lentulus in Lucania while he moved against M'. Curius Dentatus near Maleventum before the two consuls could unite. Curius stayed in a fortified camp on strong ground. Plutarch (Pyrrhus 25) says Pyrrhus tried a night march with his best troops and the strongest elephants over the wooded heights, to fall on the Roman camp from above at dawn. The march went wrong: the torches burned out, the column lost its way in the thickets, and it arrived on the heights in daylight, exhausted.

Curius led his men out of the camp against the tired troops descending from the heights and routed them. Dionysius and Plutarch say some of the elephants were captured. This first success gave the Romans confidence to come down into the plain and offer battle to the rest of Pyrrhus' army.

phases.t: Battle in the plain: elephants drive back a wing
phases.text: On level ground Pyrrhus' phalanx and elephants had the better of it on one wing, which was driven back towards the Roman camp. Plutarch says Curius then called up the guards left at the camp, fresh men posted on the rampart.

phases.t: Missiles from the rampart and the wounded calf
phases.text: The camp guards showered the elephants with javelins at close range. Dionysius and Florus tell of a calf wounded in the head whose mother turned back to it, throwing the other beasts into confusion; they ran back through Pyrrhus' own lines. The phalanx broke. Two elephants were killed and eight captured, and four of them were led in Curius' triumph, the first elephants seen in Rome. Pyrrhus left Italy for Epirus later that year, leaving a garrison in Tarentum.

tactics.note: The sources are thin and partly anecdotal. The camp, the heights and the route of the night march are inferred; the sequence of a night-march failure followed by a pitched battle follows Plutarch, with the elephant calf from Dionysius and Florus. Some modern scholars think the 'battle' was little more than the defeat of the night column and a wider engagement in which Pyrrhus disengaged.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Champion, Pyrrhus of Epirus (2009)

tactics.title: Mylae: the corvus
tactics.scaleNote: sea area perhaps 6 km across; schematic

phases.text: The new Roman fleet of 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes had been built in about two months, and its crews trained on benches ashore. Polybius (1.22) says that because the ships were clumsy, someone suggested the corvus: a boarding bridge about 1.2 m wide and 11 m long, hinged on a pole in the bows, with an iron spike underneath that drove into an enemy deck when the bridge was dropped. Hannibal (son of Gisco) brought 130 ships from Panormus. Despising Roman seamanship, the Carthaginians came on bows-first without forming line, expecting easy prizes.

The leading 30 Carthaginian ships rammed or came alongside, and the corvi fell on them. Roman marines ran across and the fight turned into an infantry action on deck, which the Romans won. All 30 ships were taken, including the flagship, a 'seven' that had once been Pyrrhus'. Hannibal escaped in a small boat.

phases.t: The attempt to take them from the flank
phases.text: The rest of the fleet tried to sweep round and strike the Romans on the beam and stern, avoiding the bows. Polybius says the bridges could be swung round in any direction, so wherever the Carthaginians closed they were grappled. They lost more ships, about 50 in all.

The survivors broke off and fled west. Polybius puts the loss at 50 ships; the restored inscription on Duilius' rostral column in the Forum claims 31 captured and 13 sunk, and gold, silver and bronze taken. Duilius got the first naval triumph and the right to be escorted home from dinner by a torch-bearer and a piper. Rome held the sea off northern Sicily for the next four years.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 1.22-23. The position of the action off Mylae and the directions of approach (Carthaginians from Panormus to the west, Romans from Messana in the east) are reasonable inferences. Polybius gives no Roman formation. The corvus' dimensions and mechanism are reconstructed from his description and debated (Wallinga 1956).
scholarship: Wallinga, The Boarding-Bridge of the Romans (1956)
Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (2000)

tactics.title: Ecnomus: the Roman triangle
tactics.scaleNote: sea area perhaps 15 km across; not to scale

phases.text: Polybius (1.26) gives 330 Roman ships with 140,000 men and 350 Carthaginian ships with 150,000, the largest naval battle of antiquity by numbers engaged if his figures are right. The Romans, heading west along the coast to cross to Africa, sailed in four squadrons: the first and second in a wedge with the two consuls' sixes at the point, the third forming the base of the triangle and towing the horse transports, the fourth (the triarii) in a long line behind, overlapping it on both sides. The Carthaginians formed a single line facing east, with Hanno's right extended far out to sea and the left angled towards the shore.

Hamilcar's plan was to break up the Roman formation. His centre turned and pulled back, and the first and second squadrons, under both consuls, pursued it westward. This split the Roman fleet: the third squadron, slowed by its tows, and the fourth fell behind.

Now three fights went on at once. In the west the consuls engaged Hamilcar's centre. Hanno's right came in from seaward on the triarii, and the Carthaginian left swung round and attacked the third squadron, which cast off the transports and fought. Polybius says the Carthaginians had the advantage in speed, but the corvus made every contact a boarding action, which favoured the Romans.

phases.t: Regulus returns; the inshore wing trapped
phases.text: Hamilcar's centre was beaten and fled. Manlius stayed to secure the prizes while Regulus turned back to help the triarii and the transports. Hanno, seeing him come, broke off and made for the open sea. Regulus and Manlius then pinned the Carthaginian left against the shore, where the third squadron had been holding it, and took 50 ships with their crews. Polybius' totals: 30 Carthaginian ships sunk and 64 captured; 24 Roman ships sunk and none taken.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 1.25-28, who probably drew on Philinus and Fabius Pictor. The battle took place off Cape Ecnomus near Licata; Polybius' numbers of ships are accepted by many scholars and the crews by fewer. The geometry of the triangle follows his description; the extent of the Carthaginian line and the exact location of each fight are schematic.
scholarship: Tarn, 'The Fleets of the First Punic War', JHS 27 (1907)
Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Tipps, 'The Battle of Ecnomus', Historia 34 (1985)

tactics.title: The Bagradas plain: Xanthippus' elephants

phases.text: After the Roman victory at Adys the Carthaginians hired a Spartan mercenary, Xanthippus, who told them their defeats came from fighting in hills where their cavalry and elephants were useless. He drilled the army outside the city and led it onto open level ground. Polybius (1.33) gives his line: about 100 elephants in a single line in front, the citizen phalanx behind them, mercenaries on the right, and the 4,000 cavalry with light troops on both wings. Regulus, with about 15,000 foot and 500 horse, put the velites in front and the legions behind them, deeper and narrower than usual to absorb the elephants, with the cavalry on both wings.

phases.t: Cavalry routed; the Roman left breaks the mercenaries
phases.text: The Carthaginian cavalry, eight times as numerous, swept the Roman horse off both wings. On the Roman left, about 2,000 men, partly to avoid the elephants, charged the mercenaries on the Carthaginian right, routed them and chased them back to their camp. This was the only Roman success of the day, and it took those men out of the battle.

The elephants charged the main Roman body. The velites and front ranks were trampled, though the deep formation held for a time. The Roman troops who pushed through the elephants found the Carthaginian phalanx waiting fresh and in order, and were cut down.

The Carthaginian cavalry, back from the pursuit, closed on the flanks and rear. Polybius says most of the Roman army was trampled by elephants or shot down by cavalry where it stood. About 500 men were captured with Regulus. The 2,000 who had routed the mercenaries escaped to Aspis (Clupea). Carthaginian losses were about 800 mercenaries. Polybius draws the moral that one man's judgment had beaten an army that had seemed invincible days before.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 1.33-34. The location on the plain near Tunis is not fixed, and modern labels vary (Tunes, Bagradas). Polybius' account of the wings is clear; the elephant line's frontage and the number of elephants (c. 100) are his figures. The Regulus legend (his embassy, return and torture) belongs to later Roman tradition and is not part of this battle.
scholarship: Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)

tactics.title: The Trebia: Mago's ambush

phases.t: The Numidians draw the Romans over the river
phases.text: It was the winter solstice season, with snow falling. Hannibal had hidden his brother Mago with 1,000 picked foot and 1,000 horse in a watercourse with high, overgrown banks on the flank of the ground he meant to fight on. At dawn he sent the Numidian cavalry across the Trebia to skirmish at the Roman camp. The consul Ti. Sempronius Longus, eager for a victory before his year ended, sent out first his cavalry and then the whole army, before the men had eaten. Polybius (3.72) says they waded the river chest-deep in icy water. Hannibal's men had eaten and oiled themselves by their fires.

On the west bank the Romans formed the normal triple line: 16,000 Romans and 20,000 allies, with 4,000 cavalry on the wings. Hannibal had his 8,000 light troops in front, a single line of about 20,000 Iberians, Celts and Africans, and 10,000 cavalry divided between the wings, with the elephants in front of the wings. The Numidians fell back to their wing. The light troops opened the battle, and the velites, who had used up many of their javelins against the Numidians that morning, were driven in.

phases.t: Cavalry routed; Mago strikes the rear
phases.text: The Carthaginian cavalry, outnumbering the Roman 10,000 to 4,000, drove both Roman wings off the field, helped by the elephants, whose smell and noise panicked the horses. The light troops and Numidians then fell on the exposed flanks of the infantry. At this point Mago came out of the watercourse and attacked the Roman rear. Polybius notes that the elephants did great damage to the flanks.

The Roman centre, about 10,000 men, cut its way through the Celts and part of the Africans in front of it. Seeing that the river and the rain made it impossible to go back to the camp, these men marched in good order to Placentia. The rest of the army, on the wings, was destroyed between the river, the elephants and the cavalry. Carthaginian losses fell mainly on the Celts; but almost all the elephants died in the cold that followed. Sempronius reported the defeat to Rome as a battle lost to the weather.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 3.71-74. The battle was fought on the west (left) bank of the Trebia south of Placentia; the drawing is rotated so that the Roman advance (westward) runs up the page and north is to the right. The location of Mago's watercourse is unknown and is placed on the southern flank by inference; Livy 21.54 puts it between the armies.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (2000)

tactics.title: Trasimene: the ambush in the fog

units.label: Column: Flaminius with the main body

phases.text: Hannibal had marched past Flaminius at Arretium, burning the countryside to provoke him. Polybius (3.83) describes the trap: a narrow pass at the western end of the lake opening into a plain under hills, with a hill closing the eastern end. Hannibal camped on that far hill with his Africans and Iberians, put the Balearics and light infantry behind the hills along the north side, and the cavalry and Celts behind the hills near the entrance, so that they could close it behind the Romans. Flaminius camped by the lake the evening before, without reconnoitring, and entered the pass at dawn in a thick mist off the lake.

When the head of the column reached the Africans and the rest was strung out along the shore, Hannibal gave the signal to all the ambush parties at once. They came down from several directions out of the fog. Polybius says the Romans could not see where the attack was coming from and were killed in column before most could form a line or even draw their weapons. The cavalry and Celts closed the entrance.

Fighting went on for about three hours, in isolated groups. Livy (22.6) says the consul tried to rally his men and was killed by an Insubrian horseman named Ducarius, who recognised him from the Gallic campaign of 223. Many Romans were driven into the lake and drowned or were killed trying to swim with their armour; others waded in up to their necks and were cut down by the cavalry. Polybius gives about 15,000 dead.

The 6,000 men at the head of the column fought their way through and over the hill at the far end. They did not know what had happened behind them until the fog lifted. They took refuge in an Etruscan village, where Maharbal surrounded them the next day and they surrendered on terms; Hannibal kept the Romans and released the Italian allies without ransom, part of his campaign to break up Rome's alliance. Hannibal lost about 1,500 men, mostly Celts. A few days later Maharbal also destroyed 4,000 cavalry sent ahead by the other consul.

tactics.note: Polybius' topography is clear in outline but has been fitted to the ground in several ways: the traditional view puts the battle in the Tuoro plain between Borghetto and Passignano; others (Pareti, Susini) place it farther east near Passignano or in the valley towards Sanguineto. The lake shore has receded since antiquity. Positions follow the Tuoro reconstruction and are schematic.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Susini, Ricerche sulla battaglia del Trasimeno (1960)

tactics.title: Cannae: the double envelopment

units.label: Roman and allied infantry (c. 55,000), very deep
Celts and Iberians in a forward crescent

phases.text: The Romans formed with their right on the Aufidus, facing south. Polybius (3.113) says they made the maniples deeper than their frontage and closed up the intervals: the plan was to smash the Carthaginian centre by weight. The 2,400 Roman cavalry under Paullus stood between the infantry and the river; the 3,600 allied cavalry under Varro held the open left. Hannibal put the Iberian and Celtic cavalry under Hasdrubal by the river and the Numidians on his right. In the centre he advanced the Celts and Iberians in a crescent bulging towards the enemy, with the African infantry, armed with captured Roman equipment, in deep columns at each end.

phases.t: The cavalry by the river; the crescent gives way
phases.text: On the narrow ground by the river, with no room to manoeuvre, the Iberian and Celtic horse met the Roman cavalry head on. Polybius says the men dismounted and fought on foot, and the Roman horse was destroyed or driven along the river. In the centre the Roman infantry pushed the crescent back. It did not break: it bent from convex to concave, and the Romans, crowding towards the centre where the fighting was, pressed into the pocket between the two Libyan columns.

phases.t: The Libyans turn inward; Hasdrubal rides round
phases.text: The Libyans on each flank turned inwards and attacked the sides of the Roman mass. Hasdrubal led his cavalry behind the Roman army to the other wing, where the Numidians were skirmishing with Varro's allied horse in the Numidian way, without closing. On seeing Hasdrubal coming, the allied cavalry fled.

Hasdrubal left the Numidians to pursue the allied cavalry and brought his own squadrons down on the rear of the Roman infantry. The Romans were now surrounded, so packed that the men in the middle could not use their weapons. Polybius gives 70,000 dead, Livy 48,200 with 19,300 captured. Paullus died, along with 80 senators or men eligible for the senate and 29 military tribunes. Hannibal lost about 5,700 (Polybius), two-thirds of them Celts. Capua and much of southern Italy went over to him.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 3.113-116, followed by most modern accounts. Which bank of the Aufidus the battle was fought on, and the exact Roman strength (Polybius' 80,000 infantry is often reduced), are disputed. The crescent is drawn as a block pushed forward and then back; its real shape is uncertain. The 10,000 Romans left to guard the main camp across the river are not shown.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Daly, Cannae: The Experience of Battle in the Second Punic War (2002)
Goldsworthy, Cannae (2001)

tactics.title: Ilipa: Scipio reverses his line

phases.t: The pattern of the first days
phases.text: For several days the armies drew up opposite each other late in the morning and stood until evening without fighting. Polybius (11.20-22) says both sides used the same order each day: Hasdrubal Gisco put his best troops, the Africans, in the centre with Spaniards on the wings and elephants in front of the wings; Scipio put his legions in the centre facing the Africans and his less reliable Spanish allies on the wings. Polybius gives Hasdrubal 70,000 foot, 4,000 horse and 32 elephants, Scipio 45,000 foot and 3,000 horse.

phases.t: The decisive morning: the line reversed
phases.text: On the chosen day Scipio had his men fed at dawn and armed, and formed up at first light with the order reversed: Spaniards in the centre, legions on the wings. He sent his cavalry and velites straight at the Carthaginian camp. Hasdrubal had to rush his men out unfed and could only form them in the usual order, too late to see what Scipio had done until the lines were set.

Scipio ordered the Spanish centre to advance slowly. With the legions on each wing he performed the manoeuvre Polybius describes in detail (11.23): the leading units turned outward and marched in column to the flank, with the cavalry and velites in front, then wheeled to face the enemy. The aim was to strike the weak Carthaginian wings with his best troops while the Carthaginian best troops in the centre were held in place by the threat of the advancing Spaniards.

The legions came into line against the Spaniards and elephants on both Carthaginian wings while the cavalry and velites attacked their flanks. The elephants, harried by missiles from all sides, did as much harm to their own side as to the Romans. The African centre stood idle: if it moved to help the wings it would expose itself to Scipio's Spaniards, who had still not engaged.

The Carthaginian wings broke, and the whole army fell back to the foot of the hill and then into its camp. A sudden downpour stopped the Romans from storming it. That night Hasdrubal's Spanish allies began to desert, and when he tried to retreat to the coast Scipio's pursuit caught and destroyed the army. Hasdrubal escaped by sea to Gades. Ilipa ended Carthaginian power in Spain; within months Mago had left Gades and the city came over to Rome.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 11.20-24, whose description of the wing manoeuvre is precise but has been interpreted in several ways (an outward turn into column and a wheel back into line is the most common). The site near Alcalá del Río (Ilipa) is accepted; the Roman and Carthaginian numbers are Polybius' and probably high.
scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

tactics.title: The Metaurus: Nero's march behind the line

terrain.label: steep ground on the Carthaginian left

phases.text: Hasdrubal Barca had crossed the Alps and reached the Adriatic coast, but his letters to Hannibal were intercepted. The consul C. Claudius Nero left his camp facing Hannibal in Apulia and marched north with 7,000 picked men in about a week to join his colleague M. Livius at Sena Gallica. Hasdrubal noticed two trumpet calls in the Roman camp, guessed that both consuls were present, and tried to slip away by night. His guides deserted, and at dawn he was still searching for a ford on the Metaurus when the Romans caught him. He drew up with the river behind him: Spaniards and himself on the right, Ligurians in the centre, Gauls on steep ground on the left, elephants in front.

phases.t: The fight on the Carthaginian right
phases.text: The battle was fought mainly between Livius and Hasdrubal's Spaniards. The elephants charged at first and threw the Roman front into disorder, then, as the fighting thickened, ran wild between the lines, crushing men on both sides. Livy (27.48) adds that the drivers had a chisel and mallet to kill any beast that turned on its own men by driving the blade into the spine, a method he credits to Hasdrubal. Nero, on the Roman right, could make no headway up the slope against the Gauls.

Seeing that the ground in front of him made attack impossible and that the issue would be decided on the other wing, Nero took some of his cohorts out of the line, marched them behind the whole Roman army and brought them round beyond Livius' left. Polybius and Livy both credit him with the decision.

Nero's men fell on the flank and then the rear of the Spaniards. The Carthaginian army broke. Hasdrubal, Polybius says, rode into the fighting and died sword in hand when he saw all was lost. Polybius gives about 10,000 Carthaginian and Gallic dead and 2,000 Roman; Livy's 56,000 is impossible. Nero marched back to Apulia and had Hasdrubal's head thrown into Hannibal's outposts. Hannibal withdrew into Bruttium and never again threatened central Italy.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius' brief account and Livy's longer one. The battlefield lies somewhere in the lower Metaurus valley near Fossombrone and is not located precisely. Livy's names for the Roman wing commanders are used; the arrangement of the hill and the river is inferred from his description.
scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Caven, The Punic Wars (1980)

tactics.title: Zama: elephants, lanes and three lines

phases.text: Polybius (15.9-11) describes both orders. Scipio set his maniples not in the usual checkerboard but one behind another, leaving open lanes through the army, which he filled with velites who were told to retire down them or to the sides when the elephants came. Laelius had the Italian cavalry on the left, Masinissa his Numidians on the right. Hannibal put more than 80 elephants in front, then a first line of mercenaries (Ligurians, Celts, Balearics, Moors, about 12,000), a second of Libyans and Carthaginian citizens, and, more than a stade behind, his veterans from Italy. Carthaginian cavalry stood on his right, Numidian allies on his left.

phases.t: The elephant charge and the cavalry battle
phases.text: Roman trumpets and horns blew all at once and some of the elephants panicked and turned back into the Numidian cavalry on Hannibal's left, which Masinissa then routed. The rest charged the velites; many went harmlessly down the lanes and out of the back of the Roman army, others veered off to the right and left under missile fire. Those on the Roman left ran into the Carthaginian cavalry, and Laelius charged and broke it. Both Roman cavalry wings chased their opponents off the field.

phases.t: The infantry: first and second lines
phases.text: The hastati met the mercenaries and, after a hard fight, pushed them back. The Carthaginian second line did not come up to support them, and Polybius says the mercenaries, thinking themselves betrayed, began to fight the Libyans and Carthaginians behind them. The second line in turn was broken, partly by its own men and partly by the hastati, with the principes behind them. Hannibal's veterans levelled their spears to keep the fugitives from breaking into their ranks, and the survivors drifted off to the wings and the open plain.

Between the armies lay a space covered with blood, bodies and discarded weapons. Scipio recalled the hastati, had the wounded carried to the rear, and reformed: hastati in the centre, principes and triarii closed up on both wings, so that his line matched the length of Hannibal's veterans. The two lines advanced over the bodies and met. Polybius stresses that this was a fight between equals in numbers, spirit and arms, and long undecided.

The deadlock ended when Laelius and Masinissa returned from the pursuit 'as if by divine providence' (Polybius 15.14) and charged Hannibal's veterans in the rear. Most were cut down in their ranks. Polybius gives Carthaginian losses of more than 20,000 killed and almost as many captured, and Roman losses of about 1,500. Hannibal escaped to Hadrumetum and advised the Carthaginian senate to accept Scipio's terms: surrender of the fleet but ten ships, an indemnity of 10,000 talents over 50 years, and no war without Rome's permission.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 15.9-16, who knew Laelius and Masinissa. The site of the battle (Polybius' Margaron, Livy's Naraggara, the Zama of later tradition) is not identified on the ground. Appian's version, with single combats between the generals, is rejected by most scholars. Line frontages are schematic and the Roman lanes are not drawn individually.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)
Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

tactics.title: Cynoscephalae: the phalanx on broken ground

units.label: Philip: right wing of the phalanx (c. 8,000)
Nicanor: left wing of the phalanx, still in column

phases.text: The armies had been marching on parallel courses either side of a line of hills in Thessaly, out of sight of each other, in rain and fog. Philip sent a covering force to hold the crest of the Cynoscephalae ridge; Flamininus sent cavalry and velites to find the enemy. They collided on the ridge. Polybius (18.21) describes a seesaw skirmish: the Romans were driven back, Flamininus sent the Aetolian cavalry and more infantry, and they in turn pushed the Macedonians to the summit until Philip, against his own judgment, decided to commit the army.

Philip led the right half of the phalanx, about 8,000 men, onto the ridge, doubled its depth and closed it to the right, and charged down with sarissas levelled. The Roman left could not stand against it on the slope and was driven back. Polybius says that Philip, seeing his success, believed the battle won.

Flamininus saw that his left was losing and rode to his right wing. Facing him, Nicanor's half of the phalanx was still coming over the ridge in column, not yet in line. Flamininus sent the elephants straight at it and followed with the infantry. The Macedonians, caught on the move on uneven ground and unable to form, broke before they could fight.

Polybius (18.26) names no names: one of the tribunes with the victorious right wing took about twenty maniples, turned them, and fell on the rear of Philip's phalanx, which was still pressing the Roman left down the hill. The phalanx could not turn about. Its men raised their sarissas, the Macedonian sign of surrender, but the Romans, not knowing the custom, cut them down. Philip escaped. Polybius gives 8,000 Macedonians killed and 5,000 captured against about 700 Romans, and uses the battle to explain why the phalanx, irresistible on its own ground, fails when the ground or the enemy breaks its order.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 18.19-27 (Livy follows him). The ridge lies in the hills between Pharsalus and Scotussa; Hammond and Pritchett identified slightly different positions. Polybius gives no direction for the armies' approach; the drawing shows the Macedonians coming over the ridge from the north. Unit frontages are schematic.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)
Hammond, 'The Campaign and the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BC', JHS 108 (1988)

tactics.title: Magnesia: scythed chariots and cataphracts

units.label: Eumenes II: Pergamene and Roman cavalry
Cretan and Trallian light troops, Achaeans

phases.text: Livy (37.40) gives the Seleucid order in detail. The phalanx of 16,000 stood in ten divisions, 50 men wide and 32 deep, with two elephants in each interval. Antiochus commanded the right with cataphracts and his guard cavalry; on the left stood more cataphracts, Galatian and Cappadocian horse and Arab archers on camels, with scythed chariots in front. Livy and Appian give about 70,000 men. L. Scipio, advised by his brother Africanus who was ill at Elaea, rested his left on the river with only four squadrons of cavalry, kept his 16 African elephants in reserve because they could not face the larger Indian ones, and massed Eumenes' cavalry and the light troops on the right.

It was a damp, misty morning, which Livy says loosened the bowstrings and blurred the long Seleucid line, so that the wings could not see each other. Eumenes sent his Cretan archers, slingers and javelinmen against the scythed chariots. Wounded horses bolted and the chariots swung back into their own left wing, throwing the camels and the cataphracts behind them into confusion.

phases.t: Eumenes breaks the left; Antiochus breaks the right
phases.text: Eumenes charged into the disorder and routed the whole Seleucid left. At the other end of the line, Antiochus himself led his cataphracts against the weak Roman left by the river, broke through and chased the fugitives back to the Roman camp. Each army had now lost a wing.

phases.t: Repulse at the camp; the phalanx destroyed
phases.text: At the camp the tribune M. Aemilius Lepidus turned back the fugitives and Attalus, Eumenes' brother, brought cavalry from the right; Antiochus, who had lost time pursuing, withdrew. Meanwhile the phalanx, its flanks bare, formed a square and stood. The legions and Eumenes' cavalry did not charge it but showered it with missiles. The elephants in its intervals panicked and broke the ranks, and the phalanx dissolved. Livy's figure of 50,000 Seleucid foot and 3,000 horse killed against about 350 Romans is surely inflated. At Apamea in 188 Antiochus gave up everything west of the Taurus and agreed to pay 15,000 talents.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Livy 37.38-44, who drew on Polybius' lost account, with Appian. Numbers on both sides are inflated in the sources. The order of the Seleucid wings is clear in outline; the precise placement of minor contingents and of the elephants within the phalanx is schematic.
scholarship: Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)

tactics.title: Pydna: the phalanx comes apart

units.label: Macedonian left: light troops and allies

phases.text: The night before, a lunar eclipse had been predicted to the troops by the military tribune C. Sulpicius Gallus (21 June 168 by the Julian calendar). The next afternoon a fight began at the stream between the camps, by tradition over a runaway pack animal. Plutarch (Aemilius 18) says Thracians and other light troops were first into the fight, and Perseus, rather than call it off, brought out his whole army about the ninth hour.

The phalanx came on fast and in good order. Plutarch quotes Aemilius saying later that it was the most terrifying sight he had ever seen. The Paeligni and Marrucini met it first: their commander Salvius threw a standard into the enemy ranks, and his men tried to hack at the sarissas or push them aside, but were skewered or driven back. The whole Roman front gave ground towards the hill.

phases.t: Gaps open; the maniples go in
phases.text: As the phalanx advanced over uneven ground and the Romans fell back unevenly, its line began to bend and break into sections, opening gaps. Aemilius ordered his maniples to go for every gap and get in among the pikemen, where the long sarissa was useless against the sword. On the Roman right the elephants and Latin allies drove back the Macedonian left.

Once broken up, the phalanx was massacred. Perseus' cavalry left the field almost unhurt, and the king fled to Pella and then Samothrace, where he surrendered. Plutarch and Livy give about 20,000 Macedonians killed and 11,000 captured; P. Scipio Nasica, who fought in the battle and is quoted by Plutarch, put Roman losses at about 100. The battle is said to have lasted less than an hour. The kingdom was divided into four republics in 167, and Perseus walked in Aemilius' triumph.

tactics.note: Livy's narrative breaks off in a lacuna at the climax; Plutarch, using Nasica and Polybius, is the main source. The order of the Macedonian line beyond the two phalanx divisions is uncertain and is labelled generically here. The site on the plain south of Pydna (near Katerini) and the stream are after Hammond; positions are schematic.
scholarship: Hammond, 'The Battle of Pydna', JHS 104 (1984)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius III (1979)

tactics.title: Aquae Sextiae: two days and an ambush

phases.t: Day one: the Ambrones at the river
phases.text: Marius had refused battle while the Teutones and Ambrones marched past his fortified camp on the Rhône towards Italy, then followed them and camped on a hill near Aquae Sextiae, with poor water. Plutarch (Marius 19) says the fight started when Roman servants went down to the river for water and met Ambrones bathing and eating. The Ambrones, about 30,000, came on in disorder across the stream. The Ligurians attacked them first as they crossed, and the Romans came down from the heights to join in. The Ambrones were cut to pieces at the river and pursued to their wagons, where their women fought with swords and axes.

phases.t: Day two: Marcellus sent into the woods
phases.text: The Romans spent an anxious night on their hill, which had no rampart, listening to the Teutones lament. Next day Marius sent Claudius Marcellus with 3,000 men to hide in the wooded ravines above the enemy's line of approach, with orders to attack the rear once the battle was joined. He posted the main army on the hill and sent his cavalry down onto the plain to provoke the Teutones.

The Teutones charged uphill. Marius had told his men to stand, throw their pila at close range, and then shove the enemy back with their shields while the enemy footing was bad. Plutarch says the Teutones, finding the slope against them, were pushed back step by step to the level ground.

As the Teutones were forming again on the plain, Marcellus' men burst out of the ravines behind them with a shout. Attacked front and rear, they broke. Plutarch gives more than 100,000 killed or captured, Livy's epitome 200,000 killed and 90,000 captured; these figures are not credible, but the Teutones ceased to exist as a people. The people of Massilia were said to have fenced their vineyards with the bones. Marius was consul for the fifth time the next year.

tactics.note: Plutarch's narrative is vivid but topographically vague. The site east of Aix-en-Provence (Pourrières and the Arc valley, below Mont Sainte-Victoire) is traditional. The two days are shown in one frame; the position of Marcellus' ambush and of the wagons is inferred. Ancient enemy numbers are impossible.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)

tactics.title: Vercellae (Campi Raudii): heat, dust and the laager

units.label: Cimbric infantry in a great square

phases.text: The Cimbri, who had crossed the Brenner and wintered in the Po valley, asked Marius to fix a day and place to fight for the land of Italy; he chose the Raudine Plain near Vercellae for the end of July 101. Plutarch (Marius 25), using the memoirs of Sulla and Catulus, says Marius put Catulus' 20,300 men in the centre and divided his own 32,000 between the wings. The Cimbric infantry formed a square said to be 30 stades on each side, with the front ranks linked by chains; their 15,000 cavalry wore helmets shaped like the jaws of beasts and carried white shields. Marius had arranged the army so the Cimbri faced into the morning sun.

phases.t: The cavalry feint and the dust
phases.text: The Cimbric cavalry did not charge straight but swung away to its right, to draw the Romans on between itself and the infantry. Plutarch says the generals saw the trick but could not stop the men, who shouted that the enemy was running. A huge cloud of dust rose. Marius' wings, advancing, lost sight of the enemy in it and marched on across the plain for a long time without finding anyone.

The main Cimbric mass met Catulus' centre. Sulla, who served with Catulus, made sure posterity knew it. Plutarch says the Cimbri, northerners who could stand cold but not heat, sweated and held their shields over their faces against the sun of a summer noon, and that the Romans, fit and hardened, did not see the size of the enemy until they were already at close quarters because of the dust.

The Cimbri broke and fled to their laager. There, Plutarch says, the women in black killed fugitives, including their own husbands and fathers, strangled their children and then themselves; one hanged herself from a wagon pole with a child at each ankle. He gives 120,000 dead and 60,000 captured. The credit was disputed at once: Catulus' men said the spoils and the standards brought to their camp proved the victory was theirs. Both generals triumphed together, but the people called Marius the third founder of Rome.

tactics.note: Plutarch's account depends on the memoirs of Catulus and Sulla, both hostile to Marius, which explains the stress on the centre. The site (Campi Raudii) is probably near Vercelli but has also been placed near Rovigo in the eastern Po plain. The drawing is rotated: the Romans face west, so north is to the right. Positions are schematic and the enemy numbers impossible.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)

tactics.title: Chaeronea: stakes, ditches and chariots

terrain.label: stakes in front of the centre

units.label: Phalanx, with freed slaves in front

phases.text: Sulla had dug ditches on both flanks of his position to stop the far larger Pontic army (Plutarch gives 120,000, modern estimates around 60,000) from enveloping his fewer than 15,000 foot and 1,500 horse, and planted stakes in front of his centre. Archelaus had posted a detachment on the height of Thurium. Two men of Chaeronea led a Roman detachment by a hidden path above it; attacked from above, the Pontic troops fled down the slope, colliding with their own army and losing about 3,000 men.

Archelaus sent in his scythed chariots, about 60 of them, while the panic from Thurium was still spreading. The distance between the lines was too short for them to build up speed. Plutarch says the Romans' front ranks stepped back behind the stakes, the chariots crashed into them, and the soldiers laughed and called for more, as spectators did at the races in the Circus.

phases.t: Phalanx against legions; the threat to the left
phases.text: The phalanx came on, with freed slaves (Plutarch says 15,000) in its front ranks, and was received by the legions behind the stakes. Archelaus extended his right to envelop the Roman left, and his cavalry attacked Hortensius' cohorts as they came down from the heights. Sulla rode across from the right wing with his cavalry and drove them off, which drew Archelaus to shift troops from his own left.

Sulla rode back to the right, where his wing, now facing a weakened enemy, attacked and broke the Pontic left. The rout spread along the line. Archelaus' camp was overrun; Plutarch says only 10,000 of his army reached Chalcis. Sulla claimed that only 14 or 15 of his men were missing, two of whom turned up that evening. He set up trophies; Plutarch says the one on Thurium named the two Chaeroneans, Homoloichus and Anaxidamus, and remains of a Sullan trophy were found near Chaeronea in 1990.

tactics.note: Plutarch drew on Sulla's own memoirs, which minimise Roman losses and enlarge the enemy. The terrain between Thurium and the Cephissus is identified, but the exact lines are not; the ditches and stakes follow Plutarch and Frontinus. The trophy remains found in 1990 (Camp et al., AJA 1992) support the topography of the Thurium episode.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Camp, Ierardi, McInerney, Morgan and Umholtz, 'A Trophy from the Battle of Chaironeia of 86 BC', AJA 96 (1992)

tactics.title: Orchomenus: trenches into the marsh

phases.text: Archelaus, reinforced from Asia with perhaps 80,000 men, chose the flat ground near Orchomenus where his cavalry could work. Sulla's answer was the spade: he dug trenches out across the plain to cut it up and push the enemy back onto the marshes of Lake Copais. Archelaus attacked the working parties with his cavalry.

The diggers and the troops covering them broke and ran. Plutarch (Sulla 21) says Sulla leapt from his horse, snatched a standard and pushed through the fugitives towards the enemy shouting: 'For me it is a noble thing to die here; but you, when you are asked where you betrayed your general, remember to say: at Orchomenus.'

Shamed, the men turned back. Two cohorts from the right wing came up, and the Pontic cavalry was driven off with loss; Archelaus' stepson Diogenes fell fighting bravely, and the Pontic archers, pressed too close to draw their bows, used their arrows as daggers. The Pontic army withdrew to its camp by the marsh.

Next day Sulla carried his trenches right round the Pontic camp and stormed it. Many of the defenders were driven into the marshes and the lake and killed or drowned. Plutarch says that almost 200 years later bows, helmets, pieces of iron armour and swords were still being found in the mud. Archelaus hid in the marsh for two days and escaped to Chalcis; within months he was negotiating with Sulla at Delium, leading to the Peace of Dardanus in 85.

tactics.note: The topography of the Copais basin has been transformed by drainage since the 1880s, so the line of Sulla's trenches and the camp positions are conjectural. The narrative follows Plutarch (from Sulla's memoirs) and Appian; Pontic numbers are inflated.
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)

tactics.title: Carrhae: the square under the arrows

units.label: Crassus: legions in hollow square (12 cohorts a side)

phases.text: Crassus, misled about the enemy's whereabouts by the Arab chief Abgar (Ariamnes in Plutarch), marched from the Balissus into open steppe in the heat. Cassius advised a broad line to avoid envelopment; Crassus first extended his line, then changed to a hollow square with twelve cohorts on each side, each cohort paired with a squadron of cavalry, his son Publius on one wing and Cassius on the other. Surena showed only a small force at first, with the cataphracts' armour hidden under cloaks and hides, then sounded the kettledrums and revealed them.

The cataphracts tested the square and found it too deep to break, and withdrew. The 9,000 horse archers then spread round all four sides and shot into the packed ranks. Plutarch (Crassus 24-25) says the Romans waited for the arrows to run out, until they saw a train of camels bringing fresh supplies. The light troops could not drive the archers off, and the legionaries could neither reach the enemy nor escape the arrows, which pinned shields to hands and feet to the ground.

Crassus sent Publius to break the ring with 1,300 cavalry, including 1,000 Gauls from Caesar, 500 archers and 8 cohorts. The Parthians in front of him gave way as if fleeing, drew him far from the square, then turned on him with the cataphracts. The Gauls fought desperately, seizing lances and dragging riders down and stabbing horses from beneath. Driven onto a sandy hillock, Publius' men were shot down; he had his shield-bearer kill him. Of the 6,000 or so only 500 were captured.

The Parthians came back with Publius' head on a lance and pressed the square until dark. They did not fight at night, and Crassus, who had collapsed in despair, was persuaded by his officers to retreat under cover of darkness to Carrhae, leaving about 4,000 wounded to be killed. Some days later, in a parley Surena forced on him, Crassus was killed. Plutarch gives 20,000 dead and 10,000 captured; the captured standards were recovered only by Augustus' diplomacy in 20 BC.

tactics.note: Plutarch is the main source and drew on a well-informed eyewitness tradition, possibly through Cassius. The battlefield lay somewhere south of Carrhae near the Balikh and is not located. Parthian numbers (1,000 cataphracts, 9,000 horse archers) follow Plutarch's implication; positions are schematic.
scholarship: Sampson, The Defeat of Rome: Crassus, Carrhae and the Invasion of the East (2008)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

tactics.title: The Sabis: surprise attack on an army building camp

units.label: Legions XIII and XIV with the baggage

phases.text: The Nervii had learned from deserters that each of Caesar's legions marched separated by a long baggage train, and planned to attack the first legion to arrive. Caesar, warned, changed the order: six legions in light order first, then the baggage, then the two new legions XIII and XIV. The six began entrenching the camp on a hill above the Sabis while the cavalry and light troops crossed to skirmish with enemy horsemen at the edge of the woods. The Nervii, Atrebates and Viromandui were hidden in the woods (Caesar's figure is 60,000).

When the baggage came into sight, the signal agreed in the woods, the whole Belgic army burst out, scattered the cavalry and came across the river and up the slope so fast, Caesar says, that they seemed to be in the woods, in the river and on top of the Romans at almost the same moment (BG 2.19). There was no time to form properly or even put on helmets. Men fell in under the nearest standard, and the line formed by legions where they had been digging.

On the left, IX and X routed the Atrebates, drove them into the river, followed them across and took their camp on the far slope. In the centre VIII and XI pushed the Viromandui back to the riverbank. That left the camp and the right flank open. The Nervii, in a dense column, went for the exposed right, where VII and XII were crowded together; part of them swept round to the top of the hill and into the half-built camp. Camp servants fled, and the Treveran cavalry rode home to report that the Romans were beaten.

phases.t: Caesar on foot; the Tenth comes back
phases.text: In XII, all the centurions of the fourth cohort were dead and the standard lost; the men were bunched so tightly they could not use their swords. Caesar took a shield from a soldier at the rear, went into the front line, called the centurions by name and had the ranks open out. He had VII and XII close up and face outwards so they could not be taken in the rear. Then XIII and XIV appeared on the crest, and Labienus, seeing the camp from across the river, sent X back at the run. The Nervii fought on standing on their own dead. Caesar says that of 600 senators 3 survived, and of 60,000 men barely 500.

tactics.note: Caesar's own account is the only one and is written to show his calm and the soldiers' courage. The river is usually identified as the Selle near Saulzoir, though the Sambre has supporters. Relative positions of the legion pairs follow BG 2.23-25; distances are schematic.
scholarship: Rice Holmes, Caesar's Conquest of Gaul (2nd ed. 1911)
Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

tactics.title: Alesia: the double lines
tactics.scaleNote: outer line c. 21 km round; ground c. 9 km across

units.label: Camp of Reginus and Rebilus (2 legions)
Legions in the camps and forts

phases.t: The works and the first relief battle
phases.text: Vercingetorix shut himself into Alesia with about 80,000 men and sent his cavalry out to raise all Gaul. Caesar enclosed the hill with an inner line of about 11 Roman miles and, when he learned that a relief army was coming, an outer line of 14 miles facing outwards, with ditches, a rampart, towers every 80 feet and fields of obstacles: buried stakes (cippi), pits with sharpened stakes (lilia) and iron spikes (stimuli) (BG 7.72-74). The relief army arrived (Caesar's numbers, 250,000 foot and 8,000 horse, are inflated). Its cavalry fought on the plain to the west under the eyes of both armies, until Caesar's German horsemen charged in a mass and routed it.

phases.t: The night attack on the plain
phases.text: A day later the relief army attacked the outer line across the plain at midnight, with hurdles, ladders and grappling hooks, while Vercingetorix, hearing the shouts, led the garrison against the inner line. In the dark the obstacles did their work, and the Gauls were shot down from the towers. Antony and Trebonius brought troops from forts not under attack. By dawn the Gauls had failed on both sides.

Scouts found the weak point: on the north-west, Mont Réa was too large to include in the lines, so a camp of two legions under C. Antistius Reginus and C. Caninius Rebilus had been built on its lower slope, on poor ground. Vercassivellaunus, a cousin of Vercingetorix, marched 60,000 picked men round by night, hid them behind the hill, and attacked at noon, while the relief cavalry demonstrated on the plain and Vercingetorix attacked the inner works opposite. The attackers filled the ditches and climbed the rampart in relays.

phases.t: Labienus, then Caesar outside the lines
phases.text: Caesar sent Labienus with six cohorts to Mont Réa, with orders to sally if he could not hold. He himself went to the inner works where Vercingetorix was attacking, then brought more cohorts and sent cavalry round outside the outer line. The defenders saw his scarlet cloak as he came. With the Roman cavalry suddenly behind them, the Gauls broke. Vercassivellaunus was captured and 74 standards taken. The relief army dispersed that night. Next day Vercingetorix surrendered; Plutarch and Dio describe him riding out in his finest armour. He was kept for six years and executed after Caesar's triumph in 46.

tactics.note: Siege lines after Caesar BG 7.69-74 and the excavations at Alise-Sainte-Reine under Napoleon III (1861-65) and the Franco-German campaigns of 1991-97 (Reddé and von Schnurbein), which confirmed the double lines, the camps and the Mont Réa sector, though the works were not uniform. Both lines are drawn as simplified ellipses; the real lines followed the terrain. Camps and units are schematic.
scholarship: Reddé and von Schnurbein (eds.), Alésia: fouilles et recherches franco-allemandes 1991-1997 (2001)
Le Bohec, Alésia, 52 avant J.-C. (2012)

tactics.title: Pharsalus: the fourth line

units.label: Legion X (P. Sulla on the right)
Pompeian right: Cilician legion, Spanish cohorts

phases.text: Caesar (BC 3.88-89) gives Pompey 110 cohorts, about 45,000 men, and 7,000 cavalry, against his own 80 cohorts, 22,000 men, and 1,000 horse. Pompey's right rested on the Enipeus; his left, where he stood with the two legions Caesar had handed over in 50, was open, and there he massed the whole cavalry under Labienus with the archers and slingers, to sweep round Caesar's right. Caesar saw it and took one cohort from the third line of each legion to form a fourth line of six cohorts, angled behind his right, with orders to wait for the signal. He told the third line not to move without orders.

phases.t: The charge and the cavalry attack
phases.text: Pompey ordered his infantry to stand and receive the charge, expecting the Caesarians to arrive tired and disordered. Caesar criticised this (BC 3.92). His veterans, seeing the enemy not move, halted halfway on their own, recovered their breath and dressing, then charged, threw their pila and drew swords. The first to charge was the reenlisted centurion Crastinus, who died in the battle. At the same time Labienus' cavalry drove back Caesar's horse and began to wheel round the open flank.

phases.t: The fourth line routs the cavalry
phases.text: At Caesar's signal the six cohorts ran forward against the cavalry. Plutarch and Appian say Caesar told them to thrust their pila upward at the riders' faces rather than throw them; the young aristocrats, the story goes, could not bear it. The cavalry broke and fled towards the hills. The archers and slingers, left without cover, were cut down.

The fourth line swung round onto the flank and rear of Pompey's left, and Caesar committed his fresh third line through the first two. The Pompeian army broke. Pompey rode back to his camp, then, when the Caesarians stormed it, escaped towards Larissa and the sea. Caesar claims 15,000 Pompeians killed and 24,000 captured against his own loss of 200 men and 30 centurions; Asinius Pollio, who fought there, put the Pompeian dead at 6,000. In the camp Caesar's men found tables laid and arbours of myrtle. Pompey was murdered in Egypt seven weeks later.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Caesar's own account, supplemented by Plutarch and Appian (who used Pollio). Whether the battle was fought north or south of the Enipeus is disputed; the drawing follows the common view with Pompey's right on the river. Caesar's figures for Pompeian strength and losses are inflated.
scholarship: Morgan, 'Palaepharsalus: the battle and the town', AJA 87 (1983)
Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

tactics.title: Thapsus: elephants and an unordered charge

phases.text: Caesar laid siege to Thapsus, on the coast between the sea and a salt lagoon, knowing that Scipio would have to come to its relief along the narrow strips of land on either side of the lagoon. Scipio came down the coastal strip and began a camp; Juba and Afranius camped some miles away. Caesar drew up facing south with veteran legions on the wings and five cohorts of the V legion on each wing to face the elephants, with archers and slingers in front (Bellum Africum 81).

Seeing the enemy disordered and busy with the camp, Caesar's officers begged him to attack; he hesitated. Then, says the author of the Bellum Africum, a trumpeter on the right wing, pressed by the soldiers, sounded the advance without orders, and the whole line went forward. Caesar, unable to stop it, gave the word 'Good luck' (Felicitas) and rode at the enemy. The slingers and archers shot at the elephants, which turned and trampled their own men, and stampeded through the half-built gates of the camp.

On the left a wounded elephant seized a camp follower; a soldier of the V legion attacked it until it let go, and the legion later carried an elephant on its shields. Scipio's line broke almost at once. The Moorish cavalry fled first. The fugitives ran first to their camp and then to Juba's, and found both abandoned or hostile.

When the fugitives tried to surrender, Caesar's veterans, sick of a war they had thought finished at Pharsalus, killed them, and even attacked their own officers who tried to stop them (Bellum Africum 85). The author gives 10,000 enemy dead and 50 Caesarians; Plutarch's figure is 50,000. Scipio drowned trying to reach Spain, Juba and Petreius killed each other, and Cato killed himself at Utica. Plutarch also preserves a story that Caesar had an epileptic fit at the start and took no part, which the Bellum Africum does not mention.

tactics.note: The Bellum Africum, by an officer in Caesar's army, gives the order of battle in outline; the assignment of individual legions to the wings is uncertain, so they are labelled generically. The ancient coastline and lagoon around Ras Dimass have changed. Scipio's camp and line positions are schematic.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Bouvet (ed.), Bellum Africum (Budé, 1949)

tactics.title: Munda: fighting for his life

phases.t: The Pompeians wait on the slope
phases.text: Gnaeus Pompeius had 13 legions, many of them raw or ex-Caesarian, with 6,000 cavalry and as many light troops; Caesar had 8 legions and 8,000 cavalry (Bellum Hispaniense 30). The Pompeians formed on a ridge in front of Munda, with a stream and soft ground at its foot. Caesar expected them to come down to the plain; they did not, so he had to attack uphill. X legion held his right, III and V his left.

The Caesarians crossed the soft ground and attacked up the slope. The fighting was even for hours, and at one point the Caesarians began to give ground. The sources say Caesar dismounted, went into the front rank and shamed his men, and later said that he had often fought for victory but at Munda for the first time for his life (Plutarch, Caesar 56; Appian 2.104).

phases.t: The Tenth presses; Gnaeus shifts a legion
phases.text: Legion X began to push back the Pompeian left. To stop it, Gnaeus took a legion from his right and marched it across behind his line, weakening the right just as Caesar's cavalry on that side began to threaten it. King Bogud's Mauretanian horse rode round the Pompeian right towards the camp.

phases.t: Labienus' move is mistaken for flight
phases.text: Labienus led five cohorts away from the line to meet Bogud's cavalry. The Pompeians took the movement for the start of a retreat, and their line gave way. Caesar's men broke through. The Bellum Hispaniense gives 30,000 Pompeian dead, including Labienus and Attius Varus, against about 1,000 Caesarians; the survivors were besieged in Munda, whose ramparts, the author says, were built of corpses and weapons. Gnaeus escaped and was hunted down and killed weeks later; his brother Sextus survived to fight on for ten years.

tactics.note: The Bellum Hispaniense is badly written and textually corrupt; Dio supplies the Labienus and Bogud episode in a somewhat different form. The site of Munda is disputed (near Montilla, Osuna or La Lantejuela). The shifting of a legion and the cavalry movement are reconstructed from Dio 43.38 and Bell. Hisp. 31; the phases are schematic.
scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Pascucci (ed.), Bellum Hispaniense (1965)

tactics.title: First Philippi: each side takes a camp

phases.text: The Liberators had chosen strong ground west of Philippi: Brutus' camp on a hill north of the Via Egnatia, Cassius' on a hill to the south, joined by a fortified line running from the mountains to the marsh. They had the sea and their fleet behind them; the triumvirs, camped on the open plain to the west, were short of supplies. Antony, opposite Cassius, spent ten days secretly building a causeway through the reeds of the marsh to get round Cassius' southern flank and cut him from the sea (Appian 4.107-109).

When Cassius discovered the causeway he built a cross-wall through the marsh to cut it. Antony attacked the cross-wall and then made straight for the fortifications in front of Cassius' camp. At the same moment Brutus' legions, without orders, threw themselves on Octavian's army opposite them.

phases.t: Brutus takes Octavian's camp; Antony takes Cassius'
phases.text: Brutus' men routed three of Octavian's legions and plundered his camp. Octavian was not there: by his own account he was ill and had been warned in a dream to leave; Pliny says he hid in the marsh for three days. Meanwhile Antony broke through the defences, scattered Cassius' troops and stormed his camp. Each army had won on one wing and lost on the other.

Cassius, who had retreated with a few men to a hill near Philippi and could not see clearly through the dust (Plutarch says he was short-sighted), saw horsemen approaching. They were cavalry sent by Brutus under Titinius, but he took them for the enemy and had his freedman Pindarus kill him. Plutarch puts the losses at 8,000 on the Liberators' side and twice as many on the triumvirs'. Both armies went back to their camps. On the same day the Liberators' fleet destroyed triumviral reinforcements crossing the Adriatic, but Brutus did not learn of it in time. He fought and lost the second battle three weeks later.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Appian, who gives the clearest topography, with Plutarch (who used Messalla and Volumnius, both with Brutus). The camps west of Philippi astride the Via Egnatia are located; the line of the causeway and cross-wall is not. The drawing faces north, with the triumvirs to the west (left). The second battle of Philippi (23 October 42) is a separate event.
scholarship: Collart, Philippes, ville de Macédoine (1937)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)

tactics.title: Actium: the breakout

terrain.label: Preveza peninsula (Octavian's camp to the north)

tactics.scaleNote: sea area c. 8 km across; schematic

phases.text: Antony's fleet and army had spent the summer of 31 trapped at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf. Agrippa had taken Methone, Leucas and Patrae and cut the supply routes from Egypt; disease and desertion had thinned the crews. Antony burned the ships he could not man and came out on 2 September with about 230, carrying sails, which was unusual for a battle and suggests that a breakout was planned. He formed close to the strait, with Cleopatra's 60 ships behind the centre. Octavian, with about 400 lighter ships under Agrippa, waited about a mile offshore.

Both fleets waited through the morning. Around midday, when the usual north-westerly sea breeze rose, Antony's left wing moved out, and Agrippa began to extend his left to the north to outflank Antony's right. Publicola extended to match him, and the two wings drew away from the centre, opening gaps in Antony's line. Plutarch (Antony 66) describes the fighting as like a land battle or the storming of a city: three or four of Octavian's small ships around each of Antony's big ones, with fire, missiles and grapnels.

Cleopatra's squadron suddenly raised sail and went out through the centre of the line, then turned south with the wind towards the Peloponnese. Antony left his flagship for a quinquereme and followed her with a few ships. Plutarch saw this as abandonment of his men for a woman; many modern scholars think the breakout of the squadron carrying the war chest was the plan all along, and that what failed was the rest of the fleet's attempt to follow.

The rest of Antony's fleet fought on until late afternoon; many ships were burned and the rest surrendered. Plutarch says no more than 5,000 died. Canidius' army ashore waited a week for Antony and then, deserted by its commander, went over to Octavian. Octavian dedicated the site of his camp to Neptune and Mars, decorating the monument with the bronze rams of captured ships, and founded Nicopolis, 'Victory City', nearby. The war ended with the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra at Alexandria the following August.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Plutarch and Dio, both writing from a pro-Augustan tradition. Ship numbers vary widely in the sources. The positions just outside the strait between Preveza and Aktio follow the excavations at the Actian victory monument (Murray and Petsas 1989) and the usual reading of Plutarch. Whether Cleopatra's departure was planned flight or desertion remains disputed.
scholarship: Murray and Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)
Lange, 'The Battle of Actium: A Reconsideration', CQ 61 (2011)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)

tactics.title: Teutoburg: the Kalkriese gap
tactics.scaleNote: corridor c. 1 km wide; ground c. 3 km across

phases.text: Varus, leading three legions (XVII, XVIII, XIX), three cavalry alae and six cohorts from summer quarters towards the Rhine, had turned aside on Arminius' advice to crush a reported rising. Dio (56.20-21) describes the march through forest and ravines in torrential rain, the column strung out with wagons and non-combatants, attacked from all sides; the Romans built a fortified camp, burned most of their wagons and pushed on. If the Kalkriese site is right, at some point the column entered a corridor about a kilometre wide between the hill and the bog, where the Germans had built a turf wall along the foot of the hill.

Attacked from behind the wall and from the bog edge, with no room to deploy, the column compressed and stopped. Excavation at the Oberesch has found the wall, about 400 m long, of turf and sand faced with timber and with drainage gaps, built in a zigzag, and thousands of objects from Roman equipment along its foot, among them the silvered iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.

Parts of the wall collapsed, and the archaeologists found the skeleton of a mule buried under the debris, still with its bell; some Romans may have broken through. But the army did not escape. Velleius (2.119) says the cavalry commander Numonius Vala abandoned the infantry and rode for the Rhine, and was killed in flight. Arminius' men held the western exit.

Varus and his senior officers, wounded, killed themselves. Of the two camp prefects, Ceionius surrendered and L. Eggius died fighting. The legions' eagles were taken. Tacitus (Annals 1.61) describes Germanicus' visit to the field six years later: a camp with a full rampart, then a half-collapsed one where the survivors had made their last stand, whitening bones lying as men had fallen, skulls nailed to tree trunks, and altars in the groves where tribunes and centurions had been sacrificed. Augustus never replaced the three legion numbers.

tactics.note: The ancient accounts describe a running fight over three or four days; this diagram shows only the final stage at Kalkriese near Osnabrück, discovered in 1987 (Clunn) and excavated since 1989. Its identification as the place of Varus' defeat is accepted by most scholars, though some argue it belongs to Germanicus' campaign of 15-16 or covers only part of the battle. Unit positions are schematic.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle that Stopped Rome (2003)
Wolters, Die Schlacht im Teutoburger Wald (2008)

tactics.title: The defeat of Boudica

units.label: Legio XIV and vexillation of XX

phases.text: After the sack of Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium, C. Suetonius Paullinus, back from Anglesey with legio XIV, a detachment of XX and auxiliaries, almost 10,000 men in all, chose a defile with woods behind and on either side and an open plain in front, so that he could be attacked only from the front (Tacitus, Annals 14.34). The legionaries stood in close order in the centre, light-armed auxiliaries on either side, cavalry on the wings. The Britons came in loose bands, far more numerous, and parked their wagons in an arc around the edge of the plain so their families could watch.

Tacitus gives Boudica a speech from her chariot with her daughters beside her, and Paullinus a short one: ignore their noise and empty threats, keep close order, throw your javelins, then carry on with shield and sword. The Britons charged up the narrowing ground. The legion held its position until they were close and then threw its pila in two volleys into the crowded mass.

Then the legion advanced in wedge formation (cuneus), with the auxiliaries keeping pace and the cavalry, lances levelled, breaking any resistance on the flanks. The Britons, pressed back across the plain, found the way out blocked by their own wagons.

Tacitus says the soldiers spared neither women nor pack animals, and gives the British dead as nearly 80,000 against about 400 Romans; the figure is not credible but the slaughter was real. Boudica, he says, took poison; Dio says she fell ill and died. Poenius Postumus, camp prefect of legio II Augusta, which had refused to march, fell on his sword. Nero considered abandoning Britain; instead the province was punished, then treated more gently under the procurator Julius Classicianus, whose tombstone is in the British Museum.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Tacitus, Annals 14.34-37. The site is unknown: the conventional label 'Watling Street' reflects the likelihood that Paullinus fell back along the road towards the north-west; Mancetter, High Cross and sites in Northamptonshire have been proposed. The defile layout follows Tacitus' description only.
scholarship: Webster, Boudica: The British Revolt against Rome AD 60 (1978)
Hingley and Unwin, Boudica: Iron Age Warrior Queen (2005)

tactics.title: Mons Graupius: auxiliaries uphill

units.label: Caledonian front ranks on the level

phases.text: In his seventh season Agricola brought the Caledonians to battle at Mons Graupius, somewhere in north-east Scotland. Tacitus (Agricola 35) gives more than 30,000 Caledonians under Calgacus, whom he credits with the famous speech ending 'they make a desert and call it peace'. Their front ranks stood on the level ground and the rest rose in tiers up the slope; chariots filled the space between the armies. Agricola put his 8,000 auxiliary infantry in the centre and 3,000 cavalry on the wings, with the legions held back in front of the camp rampart: a victory without Roman blood would be glorious, and the legions would be there if the auxiliaries failed.

The battle opened with an exchange of missiles, which the Caledonians, with their long swords and small shields, parried skilfully. Agricola ordered four Batavian and two Tungrian cohorts to close and fight hand to hand, which suited their short swords and large shields. They struck with their shield bosses and stabbed at faces, cut down the men on the level ground and began to climb the slope; the other cohorts joined in. The Roman cavalry drove off the chariots.

phases.t: The summit force tries to outflank
phases.text: The Caledonians on the hilltop, who had not yet fought, began to come down and work round the Roman rear, scornful of how few the Romans were. As the auxiliaries pressed uphill, Tacitus says, the cavalry had become tangled in the fight on rough ground among the enemy ranks.

Agricola had kept four alae back for exactly this. He threw them at the outflanking Caledonians, who were routed as quickly as they had come on, and then sent the cavalry round from the wings into the enemy rear. The Caledonian army broke and fled into the woods, where groups turned on careless pursuers until Agricola organised the pursuit like a hunt. Tacitus gives 10,000 Caledonians killed and 360 Romans, among them Aulus Atticus, prefect of a cohort. The site has never been found; candidates include Bennachie and Raedykes.

tactics.note: Tacitus, Agricola's son-in-law, is the only source, and his account is shaped by praise of Agricola; the numbers are his. The site is unidentified, and the drawing follows his description of a slope with the Caledonian army in tiers. Positions are schematic.
scholarship: Ogilvie and Richmond (eds.), Cornelii Taciti De Vita Agricolae (1967)
Maxwell, A Battle Lost: Romans and Caledonians at Mons Graupius (1990)
Woolliscroft and Hoffmann, Rome's First Frontier (2006)

tactics.title: Strasbourg: the Primani hold

terrain.label: low rise; Roman approach from Tres Tabernae
