phases.text: Julian, Caesar in Gaul, marched out with about 13,000 men to meet an Alamannic confederation under Chnodomar, which had crossed the Rhine near Argentoratum after Barbatio's army had been driven off. Ammianus (16.12), who knew officers present, gives 35,000 Alamanni. The Romans arrived after a 21-mile march; Julian wanted to camp, but his officers and men insisted on fighting. Chnodomar commanded the Alamannic left, opposite the Roman cavalry, and mixed light infantry among his horsemen to stab at the armoured cavalry's horses. Serapio commanded the right. On the Roman left, Severus halted, suspecting men hidden in ditches and reeds ahead.

When the lines met, the Roman cavalry on the right gave way: a commander was wounded, a cataphract fell when his horse went down, and the rest turned and fled. Julian rode across with his guard and stopped them; Ammianus compares him to Sulla rallying his men at Orchomenus, and says the fugitives knew him by the purple dragon standard of his guard. The cavalry formed again behind the infantry.

phases.t: The infantry fight; the nobles break into the centre
phases.text: The Alamannic infantry charged with a roar and fell on the Roman front. The Cornuti and Bracchiati, veterans, raised the barritus, a war cry that swells from a murmur to a roar, and held, and the Batavi and Reges came up in support. A column of Alamannic nobles and chiefs, including kings, forced its way through the Roman front into the centre, where it met the Primani legion standing in reserve 'like a tower', and was stopped and destroyed.

The Alamanni broke. Severus' wing, having cleared the ambush, came forward, and the whole army pursued the fugitives to the Rhine, where many drowned trying to swim under a hail of missiles. Ammianus gives 6,000 Alamanni dead on the field and countless more in the river, against 243 soldiers and four tribunes on the Roman side. Chnodomar was taken hiding in a wood with his retinue and sent to Constantius, who claimed the victory in his own name. The army hailed Julian as Augustus; he refused, for now.

tactics.note: Ammianus' account is the most detailed narrative of any late Roman battle and is followed closely. The site lay on the plain north-west of Strasbourg, perhaps near Oberhausbergen; the Rhine is placed at the top of the drawing, which is rotated so that north is to the left. The ambush on the left is reported, not proven; positions are schematic.
scholarship: Elton, Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425 (1996)
Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

tactics.title: Adrianople: the Gothic cavalry returns

terrain.label: hill with the Gothic wagon circle

units.label: Valens with the Lanciarii and Mattiarii

phases.text: On 9 August 378 Valens, unwilling to wait for his nephew Gratian and told that the Goths numbered only about 10,000, marched from Adrianople at dawn, leaving his baggage and treasury behind. After eight miles in the summer heat the army found the Gothic wagon circle on a hill. Ammianus (31.12) says the right-wing cavalry arrived first and deployed, while the left was still strung out along the road. The Goths set the fields on fire and sent envoys to negotiate, partly to gain time: their cavalry under Alatheus and Saphrax was away foraging and had been sent for. Richomeres volunteered to go to the Goths as a hostage.

Before the talks could end, the scutarii under the Iberian Bacurius and Cassio attacked on their own initiative, went too far and were driven back. The left-wing cavalry, now up, pressed forward all the way to the wagons, but without support.

At that moment the Gothic cavalry returned with a band of Alans and, in Ammianus' words, burst from the high ground like a thunderbolt and swept down on the Roman left. The left-wing cavalry, isolated and exposed, was overwhelmed. The Tervingi came out from the wagons. The infantry, its left flank now bare, was pushed together.

The Roman infantry was packed so tightly, Ammianus says, that men could not draw their swords or pull back their arms, and the dust hid the sky. The right-wing cavalry fled. Valens took refuge with the Lanciarii and Mattiarii, who held for a while. Victor went to bring up the Batavi in reserve and found they had vanished. Valens was killed, either by an arrow among his soldiers or burned in a farmhouse where he had been carried wounded; his body was never found. Two-thirds of the army died, including the generals Trajanus and Sebastianus and 35 tribunes. Ammianus compares the defeat only to Cannae.

tactics.note: Ammianus is the only detailed source, and his account of the deployment is impressionistic. The site north of Edirne is unlocated, and the Gothic numbers are unknown. Directions are schematic; the Gothic cavalry is shown returning on the Roman left as Ammianus implies.
scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire: Valens and the Roman State (2002)
Burns, 'The Battle of Adrianople: A Reconsideration', Historia 22 (1973)
Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)

tactics.title: Catalaunian Plains: the fight for the crest

units.label: Hunnic detachment sent to the crest

phases.text: Attila, having failed to take Orléans, fell back towards Troyes, and the coalition of Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I caught him on the Catalaunian Plains in June 451. Jordanes (Getica 197-217), drawing on Priscus and Cassiodorus, describes a field rising to a ridge whose crest neither side held. Theodoric commanded the coalition right, Aetius the left, and Sangiban's Alans, whose loyalty was doubted, were put in the centre where they could be watched. Attila took the centre with the Huns, with his Germanic subjects on the wings: the Ostrogoths opposite the Visigoths, the Gepids under Ardaric and others opposite Aetius. The fighting began only at the ninth hour, Jordanes says, because Attila's diviners had foretold disaster.

Thorismund, Theodoric's son, and Aetius got to the crest first, and the Hunnic detachment sent to take it was thrown back down the slope. Then the main lines met. Jordanes calls it a battle 'fierce, confused, monstrous, unrelenting', with a stream on the field running with blood.

phases.t: Theodoric falls; the Visigoths break the Ostrogoths
phases.text: The old king Theodoric was killed, either thrown from his horse and trampled by his own men or, as some said, by a spear thrown by the Ostrogoth Andag. The Visigoths fought on, separated from the Alans, routed the Ostrogoths opposite them and almost reached Attila himself, who withdrew to the wagon laager.

Night fell on a confused field. Thorismund, returning in the dark, blundered into the Hunnic wagons and was wounded; Aetius, separated from his men, spent the night among the Visigoths. Next morning Attila stayed behind his wagons, and Jordanes says he had a pyre of horse saddles built so that he could burn himself rather than be captured. The coalition did not attack. Aetius advised Thorismund to return to Toulouse and secure his throne, and Attila was allowed to retreat. Jordanes' figure of 165,000 dead is fantasy, but the losses were heavy, and Attila invaded Italy the next year.

tactics.note: Jordanes, writing a century later from Priscus and Cassiodorus with a strongly Gothic slant, is the only narrative. The site, somewhere between Châlons-en-Champagne and Troyes (Campus Mauriacus in some sources), is not located, and the ridge cannot be placed. This drawing is a schematic rendering of Jordanes' order of battle.
scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Hughes, Aetius: Attila's Nemesis (2012)

tactics.title: Second Philippi: Brutus' line rolled up

phases.text: After the first battle Brutus held the strong position, with the fleet supplying him; the triumvirs, short of food in an autumn plain, needed a decision. Antony pushed troops south and east past Cassius' old camp to threaten Brutus' communications, and Brutus extended his line of forts southward to match. Plutarch and Appian say Brutus' officers and Cassius' former soldiers, restless and unwilling to be thought afraid, forced him to offer battle on 23 October 42, which was exactly what his enemies wanted.

phases.t: Brutus' wing advances; the other is outflanked
phases.text: Brutus led his own wing forward and drove back the troops opposite. Plutarch says the other wing, stretched thin to avoid being outflanked, was taken in the flank by Antony's men and broken, and that this happened because Cassius' veterans did not fight with conviction.

phases.t: The line pushed back to the gates
phases.text: Appian describes Octavian's legions pressing Brutus' centre back step by step 'like men moving a heavy machine', until the line broke. The triumvirs' troops seized the gates of Brutus' camp, cutting the fugitives off from it.

Brutus escaped to the hills with about four legions' worth of men, but they would not try another battle. That night he killed himself, according to Plutarch with the help of his friend Strato of Aegeae. About 14,000 of his men surrendered and were enrolled in the triumvirs' armies. Plutarch says Antony covered the body with his own purple cloak. With Brutus and Cassius dead, organised republican resistance on land ended; Antony took the East, Octavian the task of settling veterans in Italy.

tactics.note: The second battle is described in outline only, and the extended line of forts is placed schematically. Plutarch and Appian disagree on the decisive point: Plutarch stresses the collapse of Brutus' outflanked wing, Appian the frontal push of Octavian's legions. Both are shown.
scholarship: Collart, Philippes, ville de Macédoine (1937)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)

tactics.title: Dara: Belisarius' ditch

units.label: Belisarius and Hermogenes with the bucellarii
John son of Nicetas and others: cavalry (right)

phases.text: Belisarius, still under 30 and newly magister militum per Orientem, faced a Persian army that Procopius (Wars 1.13-14), his secretary and an eyewitness, puts at 40,000 and then 50,000, with about 25,000 Romans. He dug a ditch in front of Dara with several crossings: a central stretch set back, with cross-trenches at right angles at each end running forward to two straight wing ditches. The infantry stood behind the central ditch; the cavalry stood behind the wings; two bodies of 600 Huns waited in the angles, where they could strike sideways at any enemy who attacked either wing. On the first day there was only skirmishing and two single combats won by Andreas, a wrestling instructor from Byzantium.

On the second day, after the morning exchange of archery, the Persian right attacked Bouzes' cavalry, who gave ground. Pharas' 300 Heruli, posted at their own suggestion behind the hill on the left, came out and fell on the Persian rear, and Sunicas and Aigan's Huns charged in from the angle. The Persian right broke and lost about 3,000 men.
The mirranes had secretly moved the Immortals to his left. Baresmanes led them with the Persian left against John's cavalry, which could not hold and fell back.

phases.t: The Persian left cut in two
phases.text: Belisarius and Hermogenes now sent Sunicas and Aigan's Huns across from the left angle to join Simmas and Ascan, together with many of Belisarius' own guardsmen, and threw them at the flank of the advancing Persian left. It was cut in two. Sunicas killed Baresmanes' standard-bearer and then Baresmanes himself, and 5,000 Persians died. The Roman commanders stopped the pursuit short, fearing a rally. Procopius notes that it was the first Persian defeat in battle in a long time.

tactics.note: Procopius' description of the ditch is precise but has been drawn in several ways; this reconstruction (after Haldon and Greatrex) puts the wing ditches forward of the centre. Where the hill stood relative to the ditch is not stated. Unit sizes are schematic; Persian numbers are probably inflated.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War, 502-532 (1998)
Haldon, The Byzantine Wars (2001)

tactics.title: Busta Gallorum: the crescent of archers

terrain.label: small hill on the Roman left
plain of Busta Gallorum (Apennines near Gualdo Tadino)

units.label: Dismounted Lombards, Heruli and other federates
Narses and John: picked Roman troops
1,000 horse to strike the Gothic rear

phases.text: Narses, with an army of perhaps 20,000-30,000 including 5,500 Lombards and 3,000 Heruli, met Totila on the plain of Busta Gallorum in the Apennines. Procopius (Wars 8.31) describes his order: the Lombards, Heruli and other barbarians dismounted in the centre, so that they could not easily run away; Roman troops on the wings, with Narses and John on the left; 4,000 foot archers at each end of the line, angled forward in a crescent. On the far left, 1,500 horsemen: 500 to help any part of the line in trouble, 1,000 to get behind the Gothic infantry once it engaged. Before the battle 50 Roman infantry occupied a small hill on the left; Gothic cavalry charged them again and again, and the 50, packed shield to shield and rattling their weapons to frighten the horses, held.

Totila was waiting for 2,000 horsemen under Teias. To delay, he rode out alone between the armies in gilded armour with purple streamers, and performed a display of horsemanship, throwing his lance in the air and catching it, wheeling his horse. Procopius notes that the Romans had eaten while standing in their ranks; the Goths went back to their camp for a meal when the reinforcements arrived, and Totila changed into the armour of an ordinary soldier.

Totila had ordered his men to fight with the lance alone, without bows or other weapons. The Gothic cavalry charged straight at the Roman centre, leaving its infantry behind, and rode into the crescent: the archers on both wings shot into its flanks. Procopius says the Goths lost many men and horses before they even reached the Roman line, and could not break the dismounted federates.

Late in the day the Gothic cavalry broke and fell back onto its own infantry, which was carried away in the flight. The Roman line advanced and the 1,000 horsemen worked round behind. About 6,000 Goths died. Totila escaped with a few companions but was overtaken and mortally wounded by the Gepid Asbad, and died at Caprae; Procopius also records a version in which he was hit by an arrow early in the battle. Narses had the Lombards, who burned houses and raped women on the way, sent home with an escort. Teias, elected king, was killed at Mons Lactarius in October.

tactics.note: Procopius was not present (he was in Constantinople) but wrote from good informants. The site near Gualdo Tadino on the Via Flaminia is likely; the hill's position, the crescent's shape and the cavalry reserve's location follow his text schematically.

tactics.title: The Yarmuk: cavalry stripped away, infantry into the ravine
tactics.scaleNote: plateau c. 15 km across; not to scale

phases.text: In summer 636 a large Roman army, commanded by the Armenian Vahan with Theodore Trithyrios, Ghassanid and Armenian contingents, faced the Muslim forces that had withdrawn from Damascus and Emesa to the plateau east of the Wadi al-Ruqqad above the Yarmuk gorge. Numbers are unknowable: the Arabic tradition's 100,000-240,000 Romans are impossible, and modern estimates for each side range from 15,000 to 40,000. The armies had been facing each other for weeks, perhaps months, with sporadic fighting. The Arabic sources compress the battle into several days of hard combat in which Roman attacks almost broke the Muslim line and women at the Muslim camp drove fugitives back into the fight.

In the tradition followed by most modern reconstructions, the Muslim commanders sent a cavalry detachment, often named as 500 men under Dirar ibn al-Azwar, round the north end of the Roman position by night to seize the bridge over the Wadi al-Ruqqad at Ayn Dhakar, the Roman army's main line of retreat to the west.

On the last day Khalid's mobile cavalry attacked the Roman cavalry on the northern flank, separated it from the infantry and drove it off northwards out of the battle. The Arabic accounts also tell of a hot south wind blowing dust into the Romans' faces. The Roman infantry, now without cavalry support, was attacked in front by the Muslim infantry and in flank and rear by Khalid's horse.

The Roman infantry was pushed west into the angle of the ravines. With the bridge held, there was no way out: the Arabic tradition says that many were killed or fell into the Wadi al-Ruqqad, giving the name al-Waqusa to the scene. Theodore Trithyrios was killed; Vahan's fate is uncertain. The date usually given is August 636. Heraclius, at Antioch, is said to have bidden farewell to Syria ('Peace unto thee, Syria, and what an excellent country this is for the enemy') and withdrew to Constantinople. Jerusalem surrendered in 637 or 638.

tactics.note: This is the most uncertain diagram in the set. The Arabic narratives are late, partly legendary and contradictory (the 'days' of the battle are a literary scheme), and the Greek and Armenian sources are brief. The topography (Wadi al-Ruqqad, Yarmuk gorge, Ayn Dhakar) is real; the orientation of the lines, the bridge episode and Khalid's flank attack follow modern reconstructions (Kaegi; Nicolle) built on the Arabic tradition and should be read as plausible, not established.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Nicolle, Yarmuk AD 636 (1994)
